messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 74
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Editor
- Trauma Type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
- Pcl5: 77

# A Matter of Trust

Robert sits in the leather chair with his spine curved slightly forward, a posture that has become habitual over the past three years. At seventy-four, he carries himself with the careful deliberation of someone who has learned to anticipate pain. He was a meticulous editor for forty-two years—a man accustomed to precision, to catching what others missed, to imposing order on chaos. That discipline served him well in his professional life. It has not served him in love.

He met Margaret at a book club in 2021, when he was newly retired and still believing that his later years might offer companionship and ease. She was charming, attentive, seemed to understand his quiet nature. Within six months, they were living together. Within eight, the hitting began.

Robert describes the first incident with the careful distance of someone recounting something that happened to someone else. Margaret had been drinking. He had made a comment about her spending. She threw a coffee mug, and when he tried to leave the room, she grabbed his arm and struck him repeatedly across the face and shoulders. He was shocked—not just by the violence, but by how quickly his shock transformed into shame. He told no one. He told himself it was an anomaly, that he had provoked her, that he should have known better.

The violence escalated over the following months. Margaret would rage over perceived slights—a text message from his daughter, a dinner that wasn't to her liking, his quiet refusal to engage in her arguments. The physical assaults came without warning. A shove into the kitchen counter. A fist to his ribs while he slept. A lamp thrown at his head while he sat reading. Robert, who had spent his entire career finding errors and fixing them, could not fix this. Could not identify what he was doing wrong. Could not leave.

It took a fall—a genuine accident in the bathroom—for his daughter to insist on answers. The bruises on his arms and torso told a story he could no longer deny. Margaret moved out after a police intervention, though she contested nothing, seemed almost to disappear from his life as abruptly as she had entered it.

Now, three years later, Robert lives in a small apartment overlooking the harbor. He is alone by choice, though loneliness has become his constant companion. His sleep is fragmented; he wakes at three in the morning with his heart racing, certain he hears someone in his apartment. When his daughter visits, he flinches if she moves too quickly. He has stopped attending his book club. The thought of being in a room with people he knows, of having to perform normalcy, exhausts him before he even considers going.

He startles easily. A door closing makes him jump. He finds himself replaying moments from those months—searching for the exact instant when he should have recognized the danger, when a different choice might have prevented everything that followed. He reviews conversations obsessively, as if he were editing a manuscript, looking for the flaw in his own dialogue, his own character.

His editor's mind, once so reliable, now works against him. He catches himself analyzing people's faces for signs of anger, their tone of voice for shifts toward contempt. Trust, he has learned, is not something that can be simply restored through willpower or time. It is more like a manuscript that has been so thoroughly marked up that the original text becomes almost unreadable.

Robert is not yet sure whether he will ever feel safe again.
